title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP) is a rapid, noninvasive intervention used to treat hemodynamically unstable bradyarrhythmias and other clinically significant conduction disturbances. These conditions commonly result from ischemic heart disease, acute myocardial infarction, medication toxicity, electrolyte abnormalities, degenerative conduction system disease, or heightened vagal tone. Affected patients may present with hypotension, altered mental status, chest pain, dyspnea, syncope, or signs of shock attributable to inadequate cardiac output. TCP delivers electrical impulses through cutaneous electrode pads to achieve myocardial depolarization and temporary cardiac pacing. TCP is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia that is unresponsive to pharmacologic therapy and certain high-grade atrioventricular blocks.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Relative contraindications are limited but include situations in which pacing is unlikely to achieve capture or when immediate transvenous pacing is available and feasible. Challenges include patient discomfort, failure of electrical or mechanical capture, and interference with monitoring. Potential complications include skin injury and arrhythmia induction. Without timely intervention, persistent bradyarrhythmia may progress to cardiovascular collapse, organ hypoperfusion, and death. This activity reviews the indications, contraindications, preparation, technique, and potential complications of transcutaneous pacing. This activity also provides healthcare providers with the knowledge and skills needed to identify patients who require TCP and to perform the procedure safely and effectively in accordance with established clinical standards. The activity also emphasizes the importance of interprofessional collaboration among healthcare providers, with improved proficiency supporting effective teamwork in the care of patients who require external pacing.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify patients with symptomatic bradyarrhythmias or conduction disturbances requiring transcutaneous pacing based on clinical presentation and electrocardiographic findings. Implement transcutaneous pacing using proper equipment setup, pad placement, and pacing adjustments while monitoring patient response. Select appropriate pacing modes and settings based on patient condition and intrinsic cardiac activity. Collaborate with interprofessional healthcare team members to ensure timely escalation to definitive pacing therapies, thereby optimizing management of life-threatening arrhythmias and improving patient outcomes. title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Introduction
content: Transcutaneous pacing (TCP), also known as external pacing, is a noninvasive cardiac pacing technique used to treat symptomatic bradyarrhythmias and specific conduction disturbances, particularly in emergency and critical care settings. The procedure delivers electrical impulses to the heart through externally placed electrodes, producing myocardial depolarization and cardiac contractions when intrinsic pacing is inadequate. [1]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Introduction
content: The development of TCP is closely linked to the broader history of cardiac pacing. Early attempts to electrically stimulate the heart date back to the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when researchers demonstrated that external electrical currents could influence cardiac activity. Practical clinical application remained limited due to inadequate technology and significant patient discomfort. [2] Advances in electronics and defibrillation technology during the 1950s and 1960s established the foundation for external pacing methods. During this period, clinicians began experimenting with noninvasive pacing as a temporary alternative to transvenous pacing, particularly in emergency situations. [3] [4]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Introduction
content: TCP gained wider acceptance in the late 1970s and 1980s as improvements in pulse generators, electrode design, and waveform delivery increased its effectiveness and safety. Integration into modern cardiac monitors and defibrillators further expanded its clinical use. TCP is now recognized as a rapid, accessible, and lifesaving intervention that serves as an important bridge to more definitive pacing therapies. [5]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The cardiac conduction system is a specialized network of cells that initiates and conducts electrical impulses to coordinate depolarization of myocytes across different regions of the heart. This organized electrical activity forms the cornerstone of the cardiac cycle, ensuring orderly depolarization and contraction of the atria and ventricles for efficient blood ejection.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Electrical activity normally originates in the sinoatrial node, located in the right atrium near the superior vena cava. The sinoatrial node functions as the heart’s natural pacemaker, generating impulses that spread through the atrial myocardium and cause atrial contraction. These impulses then reach the atrioventricular node, situated in the interatrial septum. The atrioventricular node introduces a brief delay, allowing complete ventricular filling before ventricular contraction. [6]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: From the atrioventricular node, impulses travel through the bundle of His, which divides into the right and left bundle branches within the interventricular septum. The left bundle branch further divides into anterior and posterior fascicles. These pathways transmit impulses rapidly to the Purkinje fibre network, which distributes electrical activity throughout the ventricular myocardium and produces coordinated ventricular contraction. Disruption of any component of this system can lead to arrhythmias or conduction blocks that require intervention. [7]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Indications
content: TCP is the fastest method for increasing heart rate in many bradyarrhythmias and for restoring or stabilizing cardiac rhythm in selected conduction disturbances, as indicated by the American Heart Association (AHA). title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Indications
content: Unstable sinus bradycardia that is unresponsive to pharmacologic therapy Mobitz type II atrioventricular block Third-degree atrioventricular block Overdrive pacing of selected drug-resistant tachyarrhythmias, including ventricular tachycardia, torsades de pointes, supraventricular tachycardia, and atrial flutter

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Indications
content: TCP should be applied only if the patients experience hypotension, acute mental status changes, signs of shock, or compromised organ perfusion, as seen in acute coronary syndrome or acute heart failure. Administration of atropine or epinephrine may be trialled prior to initiating pacing.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Indications
content: Atropine inhibits the parasympathetic nervous system, which may contribute to a low heart rate. According to the 2020 AHA guidelines, atropine is administered at a dosage of 1 mg every 3 to 5 minutes, up to a maximum total dose of 3 mg. [9] This anticholinergic agent is ineffective and potentially harmful in patients with transplanted hearts, is less likely to be effective in bradycardia caused by infranodal atrioventricular blocks, and may worsen heart rate in patients with widened QRS complexes. Epinephrine stimulates sympathetic α1-, α2-, β1-, and β2-adrenergic receptors, and may be indicated when increased contractility and vasoconstriction are required.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Indications
content: TCP may be applied in patients with atrioventricular nodal dysfunction secondary to acute myocardial infarction, chest or cardiac trauma, infections such as Lyme disease or bacterial endocarditis, or sepsis. Unstable bradycardia resulting from electrolyte disturbances, metabolic abnormalities, or drug toxicities, including β-blockers and calcium channel blockers, may be managed with pacing while underlying causes are corrected, although pacing is not consistently effective in these cases.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Indications
content: Overdrive pacing involves externally pacing a tachyarrhythmia at a rate higher than the native rhythm to achieve organized ventricular activation and controlled slowing of the heart rate. This technique has demonstrated efficacy in medication-resistant cases of ventricular tachycardia, postoperative atrial flutter, and torsades de pointes. Recurrence was prevented in 14 of 16 cases using TCP for overdrive pacing. [10] [11] [12]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Contraindications
content: Cardiac pacing is generally not indicated in patients with bradycardia who are asymptomatic or hemodynamically stable. No absolute contraindications exist for TCP, as benefits may outweigh risks in critically unstable patients. Hypothermia and drug toxicities may cause myocyte irritation or prevent effective electrical capture. [13] A severe allergic reaction to TCP pads constitutes a contraindication to TCP; however, hypoallergenic pads are available as an alternative.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Equipment
content: Manual defibrillators, commonly present on crash carts and in emergency medical services (EMS) vehicles, provide both defibrillation and TCP capabilities. Before initiating therapy, the availability of all required cables, including those for pacing or defibrillation and continuous electrocardiographic monitoring, must be ensured. In patients with substantial chest hair, hair clippers or trimmers should be used to improve pad adhesion and optimize electrical delivery. A bedside ultrasound must be prepared, when available, to assist in confirming mechanical capture after pacing initiation. Analgesic and sedative medications should also be readily accessible, as TCP can cause discomfort. [14]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Equipment
content: Two sizes of pacing and defibrillation pads are available. Standard adult pads are appropriate for adults and older children. For manual external pacing (rather than automated external defibrillator use), adult pads may be applied to any patient with a body weight of 10 kg or more. In smaller patients within this weight range, an anterior–posterior pad configuration may be required due to limited chest surface area. Infant-sized pads are appropriate for patients with a body weight of approximately 0 to 15 kg. Appropriate pad selection, correct placement, and proper equipment preparation are essential to ensure effective pacing and patient safety.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Personnel
content: The following personnel are typically required to perform TCP in the emergency department: A physician or qualified paramedic to assess the patient, determine indications for pacing, initiate and direct therapy, and adjust pacing parameters. Nursing staff to provide continuous patient monitoring, administer prescribed medications, including analgesics and sedatives, and document patient response. Additional support staff to assist with equipment setup, pad placement, cable connections, and general procedural support.

content: In resource-limited settings, paramedic personnel trained in TCP may independently initiate and perform pacing with minimal additional staff, provided that patient monitoring and safety standards are maintained.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Preparation
content: Whenever feasible, the patient’s skin should be prepared before TCP pads are placed. Excessive chest hair should be removed to ensure adequate pad adhesion and effective electrical conduction. All metal jewelry and objects in contact with the skin should be removed to reduce the risk of electrical burns.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Preparation
content: Hair removal must be performed carefully to avoid skin abrasions, as disrupted skin integrity may increase discomfort during pacing and increase the risk of infection. After hair removal, the skin should be cleansed with an alcohol wipe to remove dirt, oils, sweat, and debris, thereby maximizing electrical contact between the pads and the skin.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Preparation
content: When multiple sets of pads are available, an initial set may be briefly applied and removed to facilitate the extraction of excessive hair, followed by the placement of a new, clean set for therapy. This approach improves pad adhesion and electrical delivery while minimizing patient discomfort. Proper skin preparation is essential to optimize pacing efficacy, reduce complications, and ensure patient safety during TCP.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Preparation
content: TCP is often painful because the delivery of electrical current through the chest wall can cause skeletal muscle contraction and associated discomfort. Analgesia is an essential component of patient care when pacing is performed in a conscious patient. Adequate pain control improves tolerance, reduces anxiety, and facilitates cooperation during ongoing therapy and monitoring.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Preparation
content: Analgesics, often combined with light sedation when appropriate, should be administered without delaying lifesaving pacing. Continuous assessment of pain, mental status, and hemodynamic stability is necessary to balance comfort with patient safety. Effective analgesia does not interfere with electrical capture and significantly enhances the overall quality and acceptability of TCP.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: The patient’s skin should be prepared before attaching the sensing limb leads. Therapy pads must be positioned on the torso while avoiding implanted devices, medication patches, and nonintact skin. Complete adhesion of the pads to the skin should be ensured.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: Multiple configurations of pad placement are possible. Traditional teaching and early manufacturer recommendations favored an anterolateral placement, with one pad placed on the left anterolateral chest in the area of the V5 electrode and the other on the right upper parasternal chest. Recent studies indicate that the anteroposterior approach may be more effective for achieving return of spontaneous circulation in the setting of defibrillation during cardiac arrest. [15] [16]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: A small study comparing anteroposterior and anterolateral placement for pacing found an association between anterolateral placement and a higher rate of mechanical capture when pads were positioned in the anteroposterior configuration. For anteroposterior placement, one pad should be placed at the cardiac apex in the area of the V3 electrode, and the other should be positioned between the left scapula and the thoracic spine. If pads are marked as negative and positive, the negative pad should be positioned to the left in anterolateral placement and anterior in the anteroposterior placement.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: The machine should be powered on, and the defibrillation function switched to pacing mode. Depending on the manufacturer of the machine, the pacing pads may serve as the sensing device, or separate electrodes may be required for sensing the intrinsic rhythm. When available, a pacing mode that inhibits pacing in the presence of intrinsic conduction should be selected. Mode selection includes “demand” pacing, in which pacing is delivered only when intrinsic activity is absent, or "VVI" mode, in which the ventricle is paced, ventricular activity is sensed, and pacing is inhibited when intrinsic ventricular conduction is detected.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: Intrinsic conduction sensing should be confirmed, typically indicated by arrows or triangles on the monitor screen, and the gain should be adjusted as needed until sensing is verified. The pacing rate should be set at 60 to 80 bpm, sufficiently above the intrinsic rate, to improve cardiac output and produce a measurable increase in palpable pulse rate.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: The pacing current should be increased in increments of 5 to 10 mA until pacer spikes appear on the monitor screen and continued until every pacer spike is followed by a QRS complex, indicating electrical capture. Mechanical capture should then be confirmed by palpation of a pulse or visualization of ventricular contraction using ultrasound. Mechanical capture may also be observed by comparing the heart rate measured by pulse oximetry or an arterial line with the set pacing rate.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: In patients who are periarrest due to bradycardia, the current may be increased to the maximum output (approximately 140–200 mA) to achieve rapid capture, and then it is subsequently reduced as tolerated. The pacing rate should be set at the lowest rate that reliably achieves capture, with an addition of 5 to 10 mA above threshold to maintain consistent capture while allowing an appropriate margin for error.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Technique or Treatment
content: If the patient is conscious, sedation or analgesia should be administered to reduce discomfort associated with TCP. [17] After stabilization, monitor leads should be maintained in place while external pacemaker therapy is ongoing. Removal of monitor leads may interrupt sensing input, leading to asynchronous pacing, increased patient discomfort, and an elevated risk of inducing ventricular fibrillation via the R-on-T phenomenon.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Complications
content: Commonly reported complications of TCP include cutaneous burns, skeletal muscle contractions, and electrolyte disturbances. Superficial injury from pacing pads resembles mild folliculitis. Muscle contractions during pacing can be extremely painful, often necessitating sedation and analgesia.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Complications
content: Despite patient discomfort, no skeletal or myocardial muscle injury, as assessed by creatine kinase, creatine kinase–myocardial band, and troponin blood levels, was observed after 30 minutes of pacing at 38 to 70 mA with rates 10% to 20% above the resting heart rate. Most cutaneous burns are mild; however, third-degree burns have been reported in neonates, children, and older patients following cardiac pacing. [18] [19] The risk of burns increases when pacing pads are applied incorrectly or reused in violation of manufacturer recommendations.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Clinical Significance
content: TCP is a rapid method for managing multiple conduction abnormalities. Conditions ranging from bradycardia to ventricular tachycardia may be treated with external pacing as a temporary measure until definitive therapy is implemented. TCP is also indicated for drug-induced electrical disturbances and conduction system inhibition secondary to myocardial infarction. This lifesaving intervention may be performed by trained in-hospital personnel during acute clinical deterioration or by EMS providers during the transport of critically ill patients to maintain adequate cardiac output and ensure sufficient organ perfusion. [20]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: TCP may be required on medical and surgical floors, as well as in critical care settings. Clinicians must closely monitor patients and be thoroughly familiar with external pacing and their indications. Before pacing is initiated, patients should be educated about potential complications, including cutaneous burns and the possibility of failure to achieve electrical capture. Patients should also be informed about possible discomfort from tingling or brief shock-like nerve impulses.

content: Clinicians must be prepared for situations in which TCP may not be effective and should ensure that a transvenous pacer system kit and appropriate medications are immediately available at the bedside.

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Documented cases of mobile phone interference with implantable cardiac devices exist. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) recommends keeping smartphones at least 6 inches away from such devices. The primary mechanism of interference involves activation of magnet mode, which is not relevant to TCP. A secondary mechanism relates to radiofrequency emissions, the incidence of which has decreased with improved device shielding and advances in mobile network technology. Evidence regarding interference with TCP is limited; however, minimizing mobile phone use near pacing equipment is recommended to reduce potential interference. [21]

title: Transcutaneous Pacing -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Studies have shown that the hemodynamic effects of TCP are similar to those of internal right ventricular pacing. However, current available evidence does not demonstrate a clear improvement in patient outcomes with TCP. Available studies are limited by small sample sizes, often fewer than 150 patients, and delays in pacing initiation exceeding 20 minutes. Larger studies with earlier application are needed to better define the impact of TCP on clinical outcomes. [22]
